Music.title: Music Genres and Instruments
Music.text:
Music genres: pop, rock, jazz, classical, hip-hop, rap, folk, Turkish folk music (türkü), Turkish classical music, electronic, R&B, opera.

Instruments:
String: guitar, violin, cello, bağlama (saz), oud, kanun.
Wind: flute, ney, saxophone, trumpet, zurna.
Percussion: drums, davul, darbuka, tambourine.
Keyboard: piano.

People: composer, singer, musician, conductor, band, orchestra, choir, audience.

Language focus, expressing preferences:
prefer + noun / verb-ing + to: I prefer jazz to rock. I prefer listening to playing.
would rather + base verb + than: I'd rather go to a concert than watch it online.
would prefer + to infinitive: I'd prefer to learn the piano.

Talking about musical taste:
I'm really into hip-hop.
Classical music isn't my cup of tea.
This song always cheers me up.
Music.q: I'd rather ___ to a live concert than listen to the album at home.
Music.explain: After would rather we use the base form of the verb: I'd rather go.

Music.title: Talking About Music Experiences
Music.text:
Language focus, present perfect and past simple:

Present perfect (have / has + V3): experiences up to now, no specific time.
I have been to three rock concerts.
She has played the violin since she was seven.
Have you ever heard Turkish folk music live?

Past simple: finished actions at a specific past time.
I went to a jazz festival last summer.
Barış Manço released this song in 1981.

for and since with present perfect:
for + a period of time: for ten years, for a long time
since + a point in time: since 2015, since childhood

Useful phrases: go on tour, release an album, perform live, hit the charts, be in tune, play by ear.
Music.q: My brother ___ the guitar since he was twelve.
Music.explain: An action that started in the past and continues now, with since: present perfect, has played.

Friendship.title: Expressing Opinions About Friendship
Friendship.text:
What makes a good friendship? trust, loyalty, honesty, respect, support, shared interests, good communication, spending quality time.

Giving opinions:
In my opinion, ... / I think ... / As far as I'm concerned, ... / Personally, I believe ...
To be honest, ...

Agreeing:
I totally agree. / You're right. / That's true. / Exactly!

Disagreeing politely:
I'm not sure about that. / I see your point, but ... / I'm afraid I disagree. / That's not always true.

Adding reasons:
because, since, as, that's why, for this reason.

Example: In my opinion, online friends can be real friends because they can support you when you need it. However, I think face-to-face friendships are usually deeper.
Friendship.q: Which expression is a polite way to disagree with someone?
choices: I see your point, but I don't think so.
Friendship.explain: I see your point, but ... shows respect for the other person's view before disagreeing.

Friendship.title: Regrets and Criticism: should have / could have
Friendship.text:
We use modal perfect forms to talk about past actions:

should have + V3: something was the right thing to do, but you didn't do it (regret or criticism).
I should have called my friend on her birthday. (I didn't call her.)
You shouldn't have told her secret to everyone. (You told it.)

could have + V3: a possibility in the past that didn't happen.
You could have asked me for help. (You didn't ask.)

must have + V3: a strong guess about the past.
She isn't answering. She must have fallen asleep.

might have + V3: a weaker guess about the past.
He might have forgotten our plan.

These forms are very useful when friends talk about misunderstandings and arguments.
Friendship.q: I forgot my best friend's birthday. I ___ it in my calendar.
Friendship.explain: A regret about the past (I didn't write it) takes should have + past participle: should have written.

Human Rights.title: Human Rights Vocabulary
Human Rights.text:
Human rights are the basic rights and freedoms that belong to every person in the world. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the United Nations in 1948.

Basic rights: the right to life, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, the right to education, the right to a fair trial, equality before the law, the right to vote, the right to work, children's rights, women's rights.

Problems: discrimination, inequality, poverty, child labour, violence, censorship, slavery, racism.

Organisations: the United Nations (UN), UNICEF (children), Amnesty International, the Red Cross / Red Crescent (Kızılay).

Useful verbs: protect, violate, defend, respect, deny, guarantee, fight for, raise awareness.

Example: Every child has the right to education. Child labour violates children's rights.
Human Rights.q: Making children work in factories instead of sending them to school ___ their right to education.
Human Rights.explain: Child labour goes against (breaks) children's rights, so the correct verb is violates.

Human Rights.title: Passive Voice with Modals
Human Rights.text:
We often use the passive with modals when we talk about rules, rights and duties, because the action is more important than the person.

Form: modal + be + past participle (V3)
Human rights must be protected.
Every citizen should be treated equally.
Children cannot be forced to work.
This problem can be solved through education.
Women's rights have to be respected everywhere.

Active → passive:
Governments must protect freedom of speech.
→ Freedom of speech must be protected (by governments).

Negative: People shouldn't be judged by their appearance.
Question: Can discrimination be stopped?
Human Rights.q: Everyone ___ equally, regardless of their religion or nationality.
Human Rights.explain: Everyone receives the action, so we need the passive: should be + past participle (treated).

Coming Soon.title: Films, Trailers and Reviews
Coming Soon.text:
Film vocabulary: trailer, plot, cast, director, script, scene, special effects, soundtrack, sequel, premiere, box office, blockbuster, review, rating.

Genres: action, thriller, horror, comedy, romantic comedy, drama, science fiction, fantasy, animation, documentary, biopic.

Adjectives for reviews: gripping, thrilling, hilarious, moving, predictable, dull, breathtaking, overrated, must-see.

Writing a film review:
1. Introduction: title, genre, director, main actors.
2. Plot summary (without spoilers!).
3. Opinion: acting, special effects, music.
4. Recommendation: I highly recommend it to ... / It's worth watching. / Don't miss it!

Phrases: It's set in ... / It stars ... / It's based on a true story. / The plot is about ...
Coming Soon.q: The ending of the film was so ___ that I guessed it in the first ten minutes.
Coming Soon.explain: An ending you can guess easily is predictable.

Coming Soon.title: Future Continuous and Future Perfect
Coming Soon.text:
Future continuous (will be + verb-ing): an action in progress at a specific time in the future.
This time next week, I will be watching the new film at the cinema.
At 9 pm tonight, they will be filming the final scene.

Future perfect (will have + V3): an action that will be completed before a specific time in the future.
By the end of this year, the director will have finished the sequel.
By 2030, people will have stopped going to cinemas, some say.
by + time: by Friday, by next month, by the time ...

Other future forms:
be going to: plans and predictions with evidence.
Present continuous: fixed arrangements (We're seeing the film on Saturday.)
Present simple: timetables (The film starts at 8 pm.)
Coming Soon.q: By the time the film is released next year, the actors ___ three years working on it.
Coming Soon.explain: An action completed before a future time (by the time ...): future perfect, will have spent.

Psychology.title: Emotions and the Mind
Psychology.text:
Psychology is the scientific study of the mind and behaviour.

Emotions and states: anxiety, stress, motivation, confidence, self-esteem, empathy, frustration, happiness, fear, anger, curiosity.

Personality types: introvert (enjoys being alone, quiet), extrovert (sociable, outgoing), optimist, pessimist, perfectionist.

Healthy mental habits: getting enough sleep, exercising, talking about feelings, mindfulness and breathing exercises, limiting social media, asking for professional help when needed.

Useful phrases:
I tend to get nervous before exams.
She is good at dealing with stress.
He gets angry easily.
Talking to a friend helps me calm down.

Body language: eye contact, gestures, facial expressions, posture. Psychologists say much of our communication is non-verbal.
Psychology.q: Someone who enjoys being alone and feels tired after big social events is usually described as ___.
Psychology.explain: An introvert is a person who prefers quiet time alone and finds large social events tiring.

Psychology.title: Reported Speech
Psychology.text:
We use reported (indirect) speech to tell what someone else said. The verb tense usually moves one step back into the past.

Direct → reported:
am / is / are → was / were
"I am stressed," she said. → She said (that) she was stressed.
present simple → past simple
"I feel better," he said. → He said he felt better.
present continuous → past continuous
past simple / present perfect → past perfect
"I have finished the test," Ali said. → Ali said he had finished the test.
will → would, can → could

Pronouns and time words also change: today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there.

Reported questions use statement word order:
"Are you nervous?" → She asked me if I was nervous.
"Why are you sad?" → He asked me why I was sad.

Reported commands: "Relax!" → The doctor told me to relax.
Psychology.q: "I can't sleep well at night," Ayşe said. → Ayşe said that she ___ sleep well at night.
Psychology.explain: In reported speech can moves back to could: can't → couldn't.

Favors.title: Asking for and Offering Favors
Favors.text:
A favour is something kind that you do to help someone.

Asking for a favour (from informal to very polite):
Can you help me with this?
Could you lend me your notes?
Would you mind carrying this bag for me? (would you mind + verb-ing)
I was wondering if you could help me with my project.
Do you think you could ...?

Accepting: Sure, no problem. / Of course. / I'd be happy to.
Refusing politely: I'm sorry, but I can't. I'm really busy. / I wish I could, but ...

Offering help:
Shall I open the window for you?
Can I give you a hand?
Would you like me to carry that?
Let me help you.
I'll do it for you if you like.

Thanking: Thanks a lot. / I really appreciate it. / That's very kind of you. / I owe you one!
Favors.q: Which is the most polite way to ask a teacher for a favour?
choices: I was wondering if you could explain this topic again.
Favors.explain: I was wondering if you could ... is a very polite and indirect way to make a request.

Favors.title: Volunteering and Helping Others
Favors.text:
Volunteering means working to help others without being paid.

Volunteering activities: helping elderly people, tutoring younger students, planting trees, cleaning beaches, working at animal shelters, collecting donations, helping after disasters (with AFAD or Kızılay), reading books to children in hospitals.

Benefits: You gain experience and new skills, make new friends, feel useful and happier, and contribute to society.

Language focus, gerunds and infinitives:
Some verbs are followed by -ing: enjoy, avoid, mind, suggest, keep, finish.
I enjoy helping children with their homework.
Some verbs are followed by to + infinitive: decide, want, hope, plan, offer, agree, refuse.
She offered to help at the animal shelter.
We decided to collect books for the village school.

Infinitive of purpose (to + verb = in order to):
They organised a concert to raise money for charity.
Favors.q: My friends and I decided ___ a book drive for the village school.
Favors.explain: The verb decide is followed by to + infinitive: decided to organise.

New Stories.title: News and Media
New Stories.text:
News vocabulary: headline, article, reporter, journalist, editor, breaking news, front page, source, eyewitness, interview, coverage, fake news, press release.

Types of news: politics, economy, sports, technology, health, science, environment, culture and arts, local news.

Media: newspapers, magazines, TV channels, radio, news websites, podcasts, social media.

Reading news critically:
Who wrote it? Is the source reliable?
Is it a fact or an opinion?
Are other sources reporting the same story?
Is the headline exaggerated (clickbait)?
Check the date and look for evidence.

Fake news spreads quickly on social media. Fact-checking websites help people find out whether a story is true.
New Stories.q: A shocking headline written only to make people click on a link, without real content, is called ___.
New Stories.explain: Clickbait is a misleading or exaggerated headline designed to attract clicks.

New Stories.title: Telling a News Story: Past Tenses and the Passive
New Stories.text:
News stories use past tenses together to report events clearly:

Past simple: the main events.
A strong earthquake hit the region yesterday.
Past continuous: background actions.
Most people were sleeping when the earthquake struck.
Past perfect: earlier events.
Rescue teams had arrived before the sun rose.

The passive is very common in news because the event or the people affected are more important than who did the action:
The bridge was damaged by the flood.
Three people were rescued from the building.
A new vaccine has been developed by scientists.
The winners will be announced tomorrow.

Headlines use special grammar: present simple for past events, infinitive for future, and no articles.
EARTHQUAKE HITS EASTERN CITY
PRESIDENT TO VISIT JAPAN
TEENAGER FOUND SAFE
New Stories.q: Choose the correct passive sentence for a news report.
choices: The thieves were arrested by the police yesterday.
The thieves arrested the police yesterday.
New Stories.explain: Past simple passive with a plural subject: were + past participle (arrested).

Alternative Energy.title: Renewable Energy Sources
Alternative Energy.text:
Renewable (alternative) energy sources do not run out and produce little or no pollution.

Solar energy: Solar panels change sunlight into electricity.
Wind energy: Wind turbines produce electricity from the wind.
Hydroelectric energy: The power of moving water in dams produces electricity.
Geothermal energy: Heat from inside the Earth (Türkiye is rich in geothermal sources, especially in the Aegean region).
Biomass: Energy from plants and organic waste.
Tidal and wave energy: Energy from the movement of the sea.

Non-renewable sources: coal, oil, natural gas, nuclear fuel (uranium).

Advantages of renewable energy: clean, sustainable, reduces greenhouse gases, creates new jobs.
Disadvantages: high installation costs, depends on weather (no sun at night, no wind on calm days), needs large areas, energy storage problems.
Alternative Energy.q: Which energy source uses heat from inside the Earth?
Alternative Energy.explain: Geothermal energy comes from the heat inside the Earth.

Alternative Energy.title: Conditionals: Talking About Possibilities
Alternative Energy.text:
First conditional: real or likely future situations.
If + present simple, will + base verb
If we use more solar energy, we will reduce air pollution.

Second conditional: imaginary or unlikely present / future situations.
If + past simple, would + base verb
If every house had solar panels, we wouldn't need coal power stations.
If I were the mayor, I would build wind farms. (We use were for all persons.)

Third conditional: imaginary past situations.
If + past perfect, would have + V3
If people had invested in renewable energy earlier, the climate crisis wouldn't have become so serious.

Zero conditional: general truths.
If you heat water to 100 °C, it boils.

unless = if not: Unless we change our habits, the planet will get warmer.
Alternative Energy.q: If I ___ a lot of money, I would install solar panels on our roof.
Alternative Energy.explain: Second conditional for an imaginary situation: If + past simple (had), would + base verb.

Technology.title: Inventions and Modern Technology
Technology.text:
Technology vocabulary: device, gadget, app, software, hardware, artificial intelligence (AI), virtual reality (VR), robot, drone, 3D printer, smart home, wearable technology, cloud storage, cybersecurity.

Famous inventions: the printing press, the telephone, the light bulb, the computer, the internet, the smartphone.

Turkish contributions: Cahit Arf (Arf invariant in mathematics), Aziz Sancar (Nobel Prize, DNA repair), Turkish UAVs (Bayraktar drones), the first Turkish astronaut Alper Gezeravcı (2024).

Language focus, describing purpose and function:
be used for + verb-ing: A drone is used for taking aerial photos.
be used to + base verb: A 3D printer is used to make objects layer by layer.
It allows / enables us to + verb: AI enables doctors to diagnose diseases faster.

Advantages and disadvantages: It saves time, but it can be addictive. On the one hand ..., on the other hand ...
Technology.q: A smartwatch is used ___ your heart rate and daily steps.
Technology.explain: be used for + verb-ing describes purpose: is used for tracking.

Technology.title: Passive Voice in Different Tenses
Technology.text:
We often use the passive to talk about technology, inventions and processes.

Present simple passive: am / is / are + V3
Millions of messages are sent every second.
Past simple passive: was / were + V3
The first smartphone was introduced in the 1990s.
Present perfect passive: have / has been + V3
Many jobs have been changed by artificial intelligence.
Present continuous passive: am / is / are being + V3
A new app is being developed by our school's robotics team.
Future passive: will be + V3
More cars will be driven by AI in the future.
Modal passive: can / must / should be + V3
Passwords should be changed regularly.

Use by + agent only when it is important to say who did the action.
Technology.q: The new science lab ___ at the moment, so we can't use it this week.
Technology.explain: An action in progress now and the lab receives the action: present continuous passive, is being built.

Manners.title: Good Manners Around the World
Manners.text:
Manners are the rules of polite behaviour in a society. They can be very different from one culture to another.

Table manners: Don't talk with your mouth full. Wait until everyone is served. In Türkiye, people say Afiyet olsun before or after meals. In Japan, it is polite to slurp noodles. In some countries, finishing all the food shows you liked it; in others, leaving a little food is polite.

Greetings: shaking hands (Western countries), bowing (Japan), kissing on both cheeks (Türkiye, France), the namaste gesture (India).

Other manners: queueing politely, holding the door for someone, apologising when you bump into someone, giving up your seat to elderly people on public transport, not using your phone during a conversation.

Digital manners (netiquette): Don't write in capital letters (it looks like shouting), respect others' privacy, think before you post.
Manners.q: According to online etiquette (netiquette), why should you avoid writing whole messages in CAPITAL LETTERS?
Manners.explain: In online communication, writing everything in capital letters is seen as shouting and can be considered rude.

Manners.title: Gerunds as Subjects and Expressing Expectations
Manners.text:
Language focus, gerunds (verb-ing) as the subject of a sentence:
Interrupting people is rude.
Saying thank you shows respect.
Chewing gum loudly in class is not polite.

Alternative form with it:
It is rude to interrupt people.
It's polite to say thank you.

Expressing expectations and rules:
be expected to + verb: Students are expected to arrive on time.
be supposed to + verb: You're supposed to take your shoes off here.
be (not) allowed to + verb: You aren't allowed to use phones in the exam.

Giving advice about manners:
You'd better not be late for the dinner.
You should always knock before you enter.
If I were you, I'd apologise to her.
Manners.q: ___ loudly on the phone in a library is considered rude.
Manners.explain: A gerund (verb-ing) can be the subject of a sentence: Talking loudly ... is rude.
